clue.text: Bob has quite enough in the bagman's bag

parts.note: a bob is old British slang for a shilling, abbreviated S
having quite enough means having an ample amount

explanation.surface: A man named Bob has plenty stowed in a travelling salesman's case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a name but is the shilling, written S in pre-decimal British money. The bagman is a commercial traveller, whose bag holds the goods he shows customers.
explanation.definitionFit: A travelling salesman carries specimens of his wares to show buyers, so what fills his bag is a specimen of stock.

clue.text: Like one in the divinity class ?

definitions.text: Like one in the divinity class ?

parts.words: Like one in the divinity class ?
parts.note: deserving worship, as a god is, rather than a pupil in a religious studies lesson

explanation.surface: Resembling a pupil in a scripture lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divinity class' suggests a school subject; it means the class of gods, beings to be worshipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Adorable literally means worthy of worship, as a deity is.

clue.text: A suggestion, that one and one make one

definitions.meaning: an idea put forward for consideration

definitions.text: that one and one make one
definitions.meaning: an offer of marriage, which would join two people as a couple

explanation.definitionFit: A proposal is a plan put forward, and also an offer of marriage uniting two people.

clue.text: Where the Birmingham graduate is beset by ten dogs perhaps?

indicators.note: beset by means surrounded, so the graduate sits inside the other letters
perhaps says the letters of ten dogs may be rearranged

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, a degree such a graduate might hold

explanation.surface: Asking where a Birmingham alumnus is surrounded by a pack of dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: TEN DOGS rearranged gives EDGSTON, with BA set inside. EDGBASTON is a Birmingham district, site of the university and a Test cricket ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The University of Birmingham stands in this suburb, so it is where a graduate studied.

clue.text: Arty type, perhaps, with floral buttons.

definitions.text: Arty type, perhaps, with floral buttons.

parts.words: Arty type, perhaps, with floral buttons.
parts.note: an unmarried man, or a holder of an arts degree, whose name also belongs to a buttonhole flower

explanation.surface: A bohemian artist wears flowers in place of coat buttons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arty type' points to a Bachelor of Arts, and bachelor's buttons is a cottage-garden flower.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bachelor of Arts is a graduate in the arts, and bachelor's buttons is the common name of several small round flowers.

clue.text: Church publication

parts.note: a public announcement read out in church, rather than a printed parish magazine

explanation.walkthrough: 'Publication' suggests a printed magazine; it is the act of making public an intended wedding, read in church on three Sundays.
explanation.definitionFit: The announcement in a parish church of an intended wedding, inviting objections.

clue.text: Bean of the low, swinging variety ?

definitions.text: Bean of the low, swinging variety ?

parts.words: Bean of the low, swinging variety ?
parts.note: the spiritual 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot' supplies a word whose letters, varied, spell a bean

explanation.surface: A dwarf bean that sways in the breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low, swinging' recalls 'Swing low, sweet chariot'; a variety (rearrangement) of that chariot is the bean.
explanation.definitionFit: The haricot is a kind of kidney bean, often dried and used in baked beans.

clue.text: Resembling Judy O'Grady's sub-cutaneous sister

parts.note: Kipling wrote that 'the Colonel's Lady an' Judy O'Grady are sisters under their skins'

explanation.surface: Looking like a woman's sister beneath the skin.
explanation.walkthrough: From Kipling's 'The Ladies': Judy O'Grady's sister under the skin is the Colonel's Lady, so resembling her is being genteel.
explanation.definitionFit: Ladylike means behaving like a well-bred woman, as the Colonel's wife would.

clue.text: It can certainly put up a resistance!

definitions.text: It can certainly put up a resistance!

parts.words: It can certainly put up a resistance!
parts.note: an electrical device that can raise or lower the opposition to current in a circuit

explanation.surface: Something that will fight back stubbornly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up a resistance' sounds like defiance; it means raising electrical resistance, which a variable resistor does.
explanation.definitionFit: A rheostat is a variable resistor used to control current, as in a dimmer switch.

clue.text: At the end *of the deluge it goes rapidly downhill

definitions.text: At the end *of the deluge it goes rapidly downhill

parts.words: At the end *of the deluge it goes rapidly downhill
parts.note: a sled that speeds down snowy slopes once a heavy fall of snow is over

explanation.surface: After the great flood, everything sinks fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deluge' suggests rain and 'goes rapidly downhill' decline; the deluge is a heavy snowfall, after which the sledge comes out. The French word luge is also hiding inside 'deluge'.
explanation.definitionFit: A toboggan is a long flat sled ridden at speed down snowy hills.

clue.text: Wherein the tree baby might get the wind up, when it is

definitions.text: Wherein the tree baby might get the wind up, when it is

parts.words: Wherein the tree baby might get the wind up, when it is
parts.note: the bed of the infant in the nursery rhyme 'Rock-a-bye baby, on the tree top', which rocks when the wind blows

explanation.surface: A baby perched in a tree could well be frightened when the wind rises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get the wind up' means be scared, but here the wind literally gets up and rocks the baby's bed in the rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: A cradle is a rocking bed for an infant, the one that falls in the nursery rhyme.

clue.text: Something brewing here behind the Iron Curtain.

definitions.text: Something brewing here behind the Iron Curtain.

parts.words: Something brewing here behind the Iron Curtain.
parts.note: Russian urns in which tea is brewed, rather than trouble brewing in the Soviet bloc

explanation.surface: Political trouble is quietly building in the Eastern bloc.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something brewing' suggests a plot or crisis; it is literally tea, made in the Russian urn.
explanation.definitionFit: Samovars are metal urns used in Russia to heat water for tea.

clue.text: Notable exercises of justice

parts.note: musical practice runs made of notes, and also the weighing balance held by the figure of Justice

explanation.surface: Famous acts of judicial power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notable' means made of notes, not famous: a music student practises runs of notes, and Justice holds her balance.
explanation.definitionFit: Scales are graded runs of notes practised by musicians, and also the balance that symbolises justice.

clue.text: It's made with craft, and tea perhaps

definitions.text: It's made with craft, and tea perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of craft and tea may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A handmade object, possibly with a cup of tea alongside.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange CRAFT and TEA together; the whole clue also describes an object made by skill.
explanation.definitionFit: An artefact is an object made by human hand and skill.

clue.text: Hawker gives us a lift at small expense

indicators.note: at shows the cheap part comes in front of the lift

parts.note: something of small expense is cheap
a jack is a device for lifting a car

explanation.surface: A street seller offers us a ride for a low fare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lift' suggests a ride; it is the car jack.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheapjack is a pedlar selling inferior goods at low prices.

clue.text: He will make the hot spot

parts.note: taken as written
'll is the shortened form of will

explanation.surface: A man is going to create a lively nightspot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot spot' suggests a fashionable venue; it is the place of eternal fire.
explanation.definitionFit: The place of damnation is traditionally full of fire, making it the hottest of spots.

clue.text: "Thrice and once the — whin'd" (Macbeth)

parts.note: the witches' line in Macbeth naming an old country word for a hedgehog

explanation.walkthrough: The Second Witch says 'Thrice and once the hedge-pig whined'; fill the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: Hedge-pig is an old name for the hedgehog, the animal that whines in the witches' scene.

clue.text: King of the frogs here in France, an Aristotelian ?

parts.note: in Aesop's fable the frogs are given a log as their king, King Log
ici is French for here

explanation.surface: A frog monarch visiting France turns out to be a follower of Aristotle.
explanation.walkthrough: Aesop's frogs asked Jupiter for a king and were sent a log.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle founded formal logic, so a follower of his reasoning is one skilled in it.

clue.text: Shower ?. Hide, then !

definitions.meaning: to shower things on someone is to throw them thick and fast, as rain beats down
an animal's skin with the fur on

explanation.definitionFit: To pelt is to bombard as with a shower of missiles, and a pelt is an animal's skin or hide.

clue.text: What the rest play perhaps, or used to

definitions.text: What the rest play perhaps, or used to

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of rest play may be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Something the others might play, or once did.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange REST PLAY; the whole clue also describes an instrument people once played.
explanation.definitionFit: The psaltery is an old plucked string instrument, largely obsolete.

clue.text: Palmist's means of saving his bacon?

definitions.text: Palmist's means of saving his bacon?

parts.words: Palmist's means of saving his bacon?
parts.note: a crease on the palm read by fortune-tellers, and also a rope thrown to rescue someone

explanation.surface: How a fortune-teller rescues himself.
explanation.walkthrough: Palmists read a crease of that name on the hand; 'saving his bacon' means a rescue, which a rope thrown to the drowning gives.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifeline is both the palm crease said to show length of life and a rope or means of rescue.

clue.text: Appropriate footwear for out-of-school activities

parts.note: soft quiet shoes suit pupils slipping away from lessons, since they help one move unheard

explanation.surface: Suitable shoes for after-school clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out-of-school activities' suggests clubs; it means creeping out of school, for which quiet soft-soled shoes are ideal.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft rubber-soled shoes take their name from letting the wearer move stealthily.

clue.text: Port as new as one can make it

indicators.note: the letters are to be made into whatever word one can form from them

explanation.surface: A harbour town as freshly restored as possible.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange AS NEW AS for the Welsh port.
explanation.definitionFit: Swansea is a port city on the south coast of Wales.

clue.text: It ' accompanied' the pussy-cat serenade

parts.note: in Edward Lear's 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat' the owl sings to a small stringed instrument

explanation.surface: Music played behind a cat's night-time yowling.
explanation.walkthrough: The verse runs 'The Owl looked up to the stars above, And sang to a small guitar', serenading the Pussy-cat.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lear's poem the owl's love song is accompanied on this strummed stringed instrument.

clue.text: Drove back, disgusted

explanation.definitionFit: Repelled means both repulsed an enemy and caused to feel distaste.

clue.text: Holy, erstwhile holey, man

parts.note: a clergyman, who in Tudor England was hidden in secret chambers in Catholic houses

explanation.surface: A saintly man who once wore clothes full of holes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holey' suggests tattered clothes; it refers to the priest holes, hiding places for Catholic clergy during the persecutions.
explanation.definitionFit: A Catholic cleric is a holy man, and hiding places built for such clergy were called priest holes.

clue.text: Scholarly Bill gets a half century

parts.note: AC is the abbreviation for account, a bill
demi- is the prefix meaning half
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A learned man called Bill makes fifty in a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a name; 'a half century' looks like fifty runs, but splits into A, DEMI and C.
explanation.definitionFit: Academic describes learning and study, the world of scholars.

clue.text: Is this Frenchman's lot an unhappy one ?

definitions.text: Is this Frenchman's lot an unhappy one ?

parts.words: Is this Frenchman's lot an unhappy one ?
parts.note: echoes Gilbert and Sullivan's line 'A policeman's lot is not a happy one', asking it of a French officer

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a particular Frenchman's fate is miserable.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pirates of Penzance song says 'a policeman's lot is not a happy one'; the Frenchman is a French police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A gendarme is a member of the French police force.

clue.text: Locksmiths and pianists are in dispensable

definitions.text: Locksmiths and pianists are in dispensable

parts.words: Locksmiths and pianists are in dispensable
parts.note: both trades work with keys, and vital staff are called by a compound of the same word

explanation.surface: Lock-fitters and keyboard players cannot be done without.
explanation.walkthrough: Locksmiths make keys and pianists play them, and essential workers are also called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Men who work with keys, and also crucial staff without whom an organisation fails.
